title: Cantilever Beam I
statement: The cantilevered component deflects too much and is over its mass limit. Redesign its cross-section to meet stiffness and nominal stress requirements while staying within the mass and packaging limits. The span, support interface, material, and applied load are fixed.

reflectionPrompt.text: Why did your cross-section change the beam's behavior? Explain how material placement affected stiffness and mass.

conceptNotes.secondMoment: The second moment of area I measures how a section's area is distributed about its bending axis. In this model, tip deflection is inversely proportional to I, and each element of area contributes in proportion to the square of its distance from that axis.
conceptNotes.neutralAxis: For these symmetric sections under elastic bending, the neutral axis passes through the centroid. Bending stress is zero there and grows linearly with distance from it, so material near the axis carries little bending stress.
conceptNotes.orientation: Rotating a rectangle or I-section by 90° changes which dimension lies along the load direction. The area and mass stay the same, but I, and therefore deflection and stress, can change considerably.
conceptNotes.massBudget: Mass here is density × cross-sectional area × length, because span and material are fixed. Within the mass limit, stiffness gains come mainly from placing the available area farther from the neutral axis.
conceptNotes.modelLimits: Results come from small-deflection Euler-Bernoulli beam theory with an educational nominal material. Shear deformation, local and lateral-torsional buckling, plasticity, root stress concentrations, joint compliance, and self-weight are not modeled. Use the results for comparison and learning, not for certified design.
